```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
has_lavaan = requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r}
library(SimplyAgree)
```

This is the second of two vignettes on the approach to method comparison developed by Bendix Carstensen in his book [@carstensen2010] and the MethComp package [@methcomp], with Lyle Gurrin, Claus Thorn Ekstrøm, and Michal Figurski. [Part 1](method_comparison_vc.html) (`vignette("method_comparison_vc")`) introduces the approach, explains how it differs from the Bland-Altman style of `agreement_limit()` and `tolerance_limit()`, and fits the variance component model with `method_vc()`. The models here, and the alternating regression for the scaled model, are theirs; we thank them for developing them.

Limits of agreement answer "how far apart are two methods?". When the methods do not agree, the next question is often "what would method B have read, given a measurement by method A?". For @carstensen2010 this is the question that matters in practice, and it is where a model for the measurements, rather than for their differences, pays off. `method_convert()` estimates **conversion equations** between every pair of methods,

$$
y_{\text{to}} = \alpha_{\text{to}|\text{from}} + \beta_{\text{to}|\text{from}}\, y_{\text{from}},
$$

with a prediction SD and prediction limits, under three models for the bias between methods [@carstensen2010]. The data are in the long format used by `method_vc()`.

We use simulated data throughout. Method B reads about 1 unit higher and 20% steeper than method A ($\beta_B = 1.2$), so the bias is not constant:

```{r}
dat = sim_methods(n_items = 40, n_reps = 3, methods = c("A", "B"),
                  alpha = c(0, 1), beta = c(1, 1.2),
                  mu_mean = 10, mu_sd = 3, tau = 0.2,
                  sigma = c(0.3, 0.5), seed = 101)
attr(dat, "truth")$conversion
```

# Constant bias: from a variance component fit

If the bias is constant, the conversion has slope 1 and its intercept is the bias, so it follows directly from `method_vc()`. The prediction SD is the SD of the difference between single measurements, and, for a method converted to itself, $\sqrt{2}\sigma_m$ (two measurements by the same method).

```{r}
fit_vc = method_vc(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                   replicate = "repl")
conv_const = method_convert(object = fit_vc)
conv_const
```

`predict()` on the `method_vc()` fit does the same thing:

```{r}
predict(fit_vc, newdata = c(5, 10, 15), from = "A", to = "B")
```

Here the constant bias is a poor description: `check(fit_vc)` shows the differences changing with the level.

# Linear bias: differences on averages

The classical approach [@bland1999; @carstensen2010, section 4.7] regresses the differences $D = y_1 - y_2$ on the averages $A = (y_1 + y_2)/2$ for each pair,

$$
D = a + bA + e,
$$

and rearranges the fitted line into a conversion equation, $y_1 = a/(1 - b/2) + y_2 (1 + b/2)/(1 - b/2)$. The prediction limits are the limits of the differences, transformed the same way.

```{r}
conv_lin = method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                          replicate = "repl", pair_seed = 1)
conv_lin
```

With replicates, each item contributes several pairs (exchangeable replicates are paired at random within item; `pair_seed` makes this reproducible), so the standard errors are cluster-robust by item.

If the spread of the differences also changes with the level, `variance = "linear"` models the SD of the differences as a linear function of the average:

```{r}
method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
               replicate = "repl", pair_seed = 1, variance = "linear")
```

**A caveat.** The slope $b$ is biased whenever the two methods have different measurement errors, because $\mathrm{cov}(D, A) = (\mathrm{var}(y_1) - \mathrm{var}(y_2))/2$: two methods with the same scale but different precision show a "proportional bias" on this plot. In these data method B is noisier than A, which pushes $b$ away from its true value. The scaled model below, or errors-in-variables regression (`dem_reg()`, `pb_reg()`), accounts for the measurement errors.

@francq2016 make this point more generally: in the Bland-Altman plot the errors of $D$ and $A$ are correlated whenever the two methods have different measurement errors, and an ordinary regression of $D$ on $A$ that ignores the correlation gives biased estimates and intervals with poor coverage. Their alternative is the correlated bivariate least squares (CBLS) regression in the Bland-Altman plot, equivalent to bivariate least squares (BLS) in the plot of one method against the other, which uses the measurement error variances (known, or estimated from replicates) and allows them to change with the level [@francq2014]; it is implemented in the BivRegBLS package. `method_convert()` does not offer this yet. With replicates, the scaled model is the better choice here; without them, `dem_reg()` with a known error ratio is the closest option.

# The scaled model

The scaled model [@carstensen2010, ch. 7] assumes that every method measures the same true value $\mu_i$ on its own linear scale,

$$
y_{mir} = \alpha_m + \beta_m(\mu_i + a_{ir} + c_{mi}) + e_{mir},
$$

with the variance components of `method_vc()`: method-by-item effects $c_{mi}$, item-by-replicate effects $a_{ir}$ (linked replicates), and measurement errors $e_{mir}$ with a separate SD for each method. The conversion from method $m$ to method $k$ is

$$
\beta_{k|m} = \beta_k/\beta_m, \qquad \alpha_{k|m} = \alpha_k - \alpha_m \beta_k/\beta_m .
$$

`method_convert(bias = "scaled")` fits this model by alternating regression (the default, `estimator = "altreg"`), as in MethComp's `AltReg()`: it alternates between regressing each method on the current predicted true values and refitting the variance component model to the rescaled measurements, until the conversions stop changing. It needs replicates, to separate the measurement errors from the method-by-item variation. For confidence intervals, use the maximum likelihood fit instead (`estimator = "ml"`; see [below](#confidence-intervals-for-the-scaled-model)).

```{r}
conv_sc = method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                         replicate = "repl", bias = "scaled")
conv_sc
```

The slope of B on A is close to the true 1.2. `summary()` shows the per-method intercepts and slopes, with the first method as the reference ($\alpha = 0$, $\beta = 1$); only the conversions between methods are identified, not the scale of the true values.

```{r}
summary(conv_sc)$scaled$methods
```

`check()` shows the residuals of the final variance component model (their normality, with Shapiro-Wilk tests, and their spread against the fitted true values, with Breusch-Pagan tests) and how the estimates converged:

```{r, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
check(conv_sc)
```

The conversion plot shows the conversion and its prediction limits with the observed pairs; the dashed line is the line of identity.

```{r}
plot(conv_sc)
```

The Bland-Altman plot shows the bias and prediction limits that the model implies for the differences, as lines that change with the level:

```{r}
plot(conv_sc, type = "ba")
```

# Transformed scales

All three models are fit on the scale set by `transform` (see `vignette("method_comparison_vc")`). The conversions are then linear on that scale, and `predict()` and the conversion plot back-transform the converted value and its prediction limits to the original scale [@carstensen2010, ch. 8]. For percentages (e.g., oxygen saturation), `transform = "pctlogit"` keeps the conversions and limits inside 0 to 100:

```{r}
sat = sim_methods(n_items = 40, n_reps = 2, methods = c("Ref", "New"),
                  alpha = c(0, 0.15), beta = c(1, 1.1), mu_mean = 1.2,
                  mu_sd = 0.8, tau = 0.1, sigma = c(0.1, 0.15),
                  transform = "pctlogit", seed = 7)
conv_sat = method_convert(sat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                          replicate = "repl", bias = "scaled",
                          transform = "pctlogit")
predict(conv_sat, newdata = c(60, 80, 95, 99), from = "Ref", to = "New")
plot(conv_sat, pair = c("Ref", "New"))
```

# Prediction

`predict()` converts values of one method to another on the original scale, with prediction limits at any level:

```{r}
predict(conv_sc, newdata = c(5, 10, 15), from = "A", to = "B",
        level = 0.90)
predict(conv_sc, newdata = data.frame(B = c(6, 12)), from = "B", to = "A")
```

# Confidence intervals for the scaled model

The intervals from the alternating regression (`ci_method = "delta"`, the default) use the standard errors from the final regressions of each method on the predicted true values. These treat the predicted true values as known, so they ignore part of the uncertainty and are much too narrow (see the table below).

For intervals, fit the model by maximum likelihood with `estimator = "ml"`. This treats the true values as normally distributed (the structural model) and fits the scaled model as a confirmatory factor model with the lavaan package, which must be installed. The alternating regression supplies the starting values, and missing measurements are handled by full-information maximum likelihood, so the design need not be balanced. The intervals are Wald intervals with $t$ quantiles on (items $-$ 1) degrees of freedom, and the prediction SDs get intervals too (on the log scale):

```{r, eval = has_lavaan}
conv_ml = method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                         replicate = "repl", bias = "scaled",
                         estimator = "ml")
conv_ml
```

The `summary()` adds the model's chi-square test of fit, RMSEA, and SRMR; a poor fit means that the normal model for the true values and errors describes the data poorly. With few items (fewer than about 20), a variance estimate can be zero or negative (a Heywood case); `method_convert()` then gives a warning, and the intervals may be unreliable.

```{r, eval = has_lavaan}
summary(conv_ml)
```

How well do the intervals cover? In simulations of the scaled model (true slopes 1, 1.2, and 0.9; 3 replicates; balanced data and normal true values; 500 data sets per setting), the 95% intervals for the conversion slopes covered the true slope this often:

| Items | Methods | Alternating regression, linked | exchangeable | Maximum likelihood, linked | exchangeable |
|------:|--------:|-------:|-------:|-------:|-------:|
| 15 | 2 | 57% | 66% | 93% | 94% |
| 30 | 2 | 53% | 65% | 94% | 95% |
| 60 | 2 | 54% | 65% | 95% | 94% |
| 15 | 3 | 70% | 73% | 95% | 93% |
| 30 | 3 | 67% | 71% | 94% | 95% |
| 60 | 3 | 64% | 70% | 94% | 95% |

The intercepts were similar. For the alternating regression, more items do not help, because the problem is not the sample size but treating the predicted true values as known; its point estimates were accurate (the slopes essentially unbiased and the prediction SDs within 1% to 2%), so its conversions and prediction limits can be used. The maximum likelihood intervals held up with 15% of the measurements missing and with uniform or skewed true values (92% to 97% coverage across all settings), and the intervals for the prediction SDs covered 92% to 95%. Its prediction SDs are a little low with few items (by 3% to 5% with 15 items), because, unlike the alternating regression, it does not adjust the method-by-item variance for the number of items.

The two fits can give somewhat different estimates on real data, especially when the true values are far from normal. For the oximetry data in MethComp, whose true values are strongly skewed, the slope of pulse on CO is 0.94 by alternating regression and 0.90 by maximum likelihood (95% CI 0.80 to 1.00), and the model's chi-square test shows a poor fit.

The alternating regression also offers a parametric bootstrap (`ci_method = "boot"`): it simulates data from the fitted model with the observed design, refits the model to each, and reports percentile intervals, including for the prediction SDs and the variance components. Each replicate refits the model, so this takes a while (the default is 999 replicates), and its coverage has not been checked by simulation:

```{r}
set.seed(2024)
conv_boot = method_convert(dat, y = "y", method = "method", id = "id",
                           replicate = "repl", bias = "scaled",
                           ci_method = "boot", boot_reps = 39)
conv_boot
```
